species.notes:
Standing order, Security Chief D. Okafor.

Do not engage critters. Most of the time they back off when the lamps come up. The ones that don't are the problem. They bite first, then swing the tail. The tail club is what killed Haskins in Gallery 4, and his suit made no difference.

Three kinds. Drudges are smaller, mostly bare bark with one patch of shell, and they're the ones you'll see foraging. Sires are fully plated and taller. The matriarch is the big one, wider than a hatch door, and she is the only one that lays. If you find eggs, she is close. Back out the way you came and call it in. Leave the eggs alone.

They weigh less than you'd think for the height, 90 to 130 kilos, so they are quick. Six eyes. Possibly weak in bright light. Not confirmed.

species.notes:
Writing this down because nobody believes me about the size.

Knee height. Maybe hip height on a big one. People hear "small" and relax, and that's how Petra got hurt. It came out of the dark on three legs, this low crawling lurch, and the armor caught my headlamp. Purple, then green, then purple again. Pretty, honestly, right up until it opened its arms.

Four arms, all claws. It went for her legs first, then put its head down and used the horns. Three horns. I counted afterwards, on the one Ruiz shot.

It has wings. I've never seen one fly. They stay folded flat against its back the whole time. Maybe they can't fly. I don't want to find out.

If you see that color on the rock, it's not ore.

species.notes:
Phoboraptor velox. Dr. M. Lindqvist, xenobiology.

The grelk is a monopod. It moves by hopping and covers ground much faster than the gait suggests; one crossed Chamber 9 in under four seconds. Standing height runs 2.5 to 4 m, mass 71 to 113 kg, so the animal is tall and comparatively light.

The pelt is long, coarse and rust red, close enough to the cavern walls that a resting grelk is easy to walk past. The hair stiffens into quills along the back and flanks. There is a single forelimb, offset to one side. Six eyes, in two rows. Adults carry branching antlers of ten tines.

Young are born live. Joeys are about a fifth of adult size, with five tines, and stay near the parent.

Grelks attack people unprovoked, goring with the antlers and biting. Please do not approach a resting adult for a tissue sample. I have now asked twice.

species.notes:
From the hydroponics crew, for whoever has night rotation.

The blobs are scared of you. That sounds like good news until you remember it's three meters tall and weighs as much as two of us, and scared things don't look where they're going. Six eyes, every one of them on you, and it still backs straight into the irrigation lines.

The skin is slick and shines every color at once. It leaves a film on anything it touches. The film does not come off tool handles, so don't bother.

Two arms with blunt nubs on the ends, nothing sharp. Four short legs. The bite is what you need to watch. Corner one and it will bite, and it doesn't let go fast.

So: leave it a way out, turn your lamp down, and wait. It'll go.

species.notes:
Deep Survey orientation. Read before your first descent.

Count the arms. That's how you tell a stingtail's age, and the age tells you how bad your day is about to get.

Grub: one arm, one leg, two little horns. Mostly a nuisance.
Nymph: two arms, still on one leg, five horns, and a tail with a stinger on it. Keep your gloves on.
Instar: three arms, now on two legs, seven horns. The tail sting can put you down. Back away.
Adult: four arms, a crown of ten horns, and a barbed sting on the end of a tail it holds up over its head. Leave the area.

None of them come up past your waist. Doesn't matter. Adults hunt people. They bite, they gore and they sting, usually all three.

The green shows up well against the rock, so most of the time you'll see one before it sees you. Use that.
